title: Many ways of being Muslim
hookLine: one faith lived in many languages, customs and schools

cards: One row at Friday prayer in a big city mosque, shoulder to shoulder. A taxi driver who grew up speaking Somali. A student from Indonesia.
A grandfather from Lahore in a crisp white shalwar kameez. A convert who learned the prayer not long ago and still watches the person beside him for the next move.
After the prayer they'll go home to different kitchens and different languages. But right now the imam says Allahu akbar, al-Fatiha is recited in Arabic, and the whole row faces the same direction.

teach.h: NATIONS AND TRIBES, TO KNOW EACH OTHER.
teach.b: Start with Surah al-Hujurat, in Pickthall's translation: "O mankind! Lo! We have created you male and female, and have made you nations and tribes that ye may know one another."
Nations and tribes aren't a problem to be solved; they're there so people can know each other. The verse goes straight on: "Lo! the noblest of you, in the sight of Allah, is the best in conduct."
Surah al-Rum lists the creation of the heavens and the earth, and in the same breath, "the difference of your languages and colours." A world of accents, on purpose.
Then schools. Among Sunni Muslims there are the schools of law named for their teachers: Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i, Hanbali. Among Shia Muslims, the Ja'fari school, and there are Ibadi Muslims as well.
In some mosques people stand with hands folded, in others with arms at their sides. Each follows a school with its own scholars and reasons. Then customs.

What's cooked for Eid, what's worn to Friday prayer, how a wedding goes: these grow from places, not only from texts. Through all of it, the center holds: the shahadah, the prayer in Arabic, the same qibla.
Sahih Muslim reports the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, saying, in paraphrase, that Allah doesn't look at your outward forms or your wealth, but at your hearts and your deeds.

how: Muslims in many countries share the shahadah, the daily prayers in Arabic and the qibla toward Makkah, while following different schools of law and keeping the customs, languages and foods of their own places.

games.q: what does “many ways of being muslim” mean?
o: one faith kept in many cultures and schools
separate religions that share a holy book
a new movement to unite all the schools

games.q: one faith, many ways — tap the pairs.
p: that ye may know one another

s: the Qur'an treats nations and tribes as a problem to be solved
it says they were made "that ye may know one another."
Muslims who stand with arms at their sides in prayer are doing it wrong
they're following a school with its own scholars and reasons, like those who fold their hands.
the Qur'an counts the difference of languages among Allah's signs
Surah al-Rum lists it right after the creation of the heavens and the earth.

games.q: you're visiting a mosque far from home. the person next to you prays with arms at their sides; you were taught to fold your hands. what do you make of it?
o: they must be doing it wrong.
they're following a different school of law.
they must belong to a different religion.
games.why: different schools pray the same prayer a little differently, each with its own scholars and reasons. the prayer, the words and the qibla are the same.

practice: Think of a place you've never connected with Islam: Senegal, Bosnia, China, Trinidad, the Philippines. Pick one and wonder, without needing answers, what Friday would look like there, and what Eid would smell like.
If you pray, remember the people of that place.

wordCard.voice: Many ways of being Muslim. One faith, kept in many languages, customs and schools of law, with the same prayer at its center. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: "nations and tribes," from Surah al-Hujurat 49:13.

carryVoice: Your line: one faith, many ways. One row, so many homes. Tomorrow, the mosque community.
